mainTopic: A mortgaged slave who was freed, a destroyed אפותיקי field, and the start of the משנה about a half-slave
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about a slave whom his master set aside as security (אפותיקי) for a debt, and who was then freed. In רב's reading, the owner freed him, so the creditor is forced to free him too. In עולא's reading, the creditor freed him, so the owner is forced to free him. In both readings, the תנא קמא says the slave writes a note for his own value, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the one who freed him writes it. For רב, the argument is about damaging someone's lien (מזיק שעבודו של חבירו). For עולא, it is about damage that cannot be seen (היזק שאינו ניכר). Each אמורא then points to a word in the משנה that the other reading does not fit. Next the גמרא discusses a field set aside for a debt that a river washed away. A ברייתא rules that the creditor collects from other property unless the debtor said 'only from this field.' A second ברייתא treats a woman's כתובה differently according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. Finally a new משנה begins about a half-slave: בית הלל say he splits his days, and בית שמאי object that this leaves him unable to marry. Their objection continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The creditor is forced to free the slave, and the slave writes a note
steps.stepSummary: Under the first explanation, where the original master freed the slave, the court forces the creditor (רבו שני) to free him fully, and the slave writes a שטר for his own value.
steps.simpleTranslation: The creditor may come and say to him, 'You are my slave.' So the court forces his second master to make him a בן חורין, and the slave writes a promissory note for his own value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its first explanation of the משנה, where the original owner freed the slave. Because the creditor could still claim the slave, the court forces the creditor to free him, and the slave owes his own value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave was set aside to pay a debt, so the creditor still has a claim on him even after the original master freed him. To keep the slave's freedom from being in doubt, the creditor (רבו שני) is forced to free him. In exchange, the תנא קמא says the slave himself writes a note promising to pay his value to the creditor.

keyTerms.meaning: His second master, meaning the creditor who holds the slave as security
A promissory note for his value, a written promise to pay what he is worth

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'second master' means the creditor, not a new buyer. Later, in עולא's explanation, the roles flip, so keep track of who freed the slave in each explanation.

phrases.english: and will say to him: 'You are my slave' –
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from before: the worry is that the creditor will meet the freed slave and claim him.

phrases.english: they force his second master,
and he makes him a free man,
and the slave writes a note for his value.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְיֹאמַר לוֹ: ״עַבְדִּי אָתָּה״ – כּוֹפִין אֶת רַבּוֹ שֵׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the גמרא's first reading of the משנה, which began before this section, where the original master freed the slave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The creditor is forced to free the slave, and the slave writes a note for his own value.

steps.title: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: the one who freed him writes the note
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees: the slave does not write the note. The master who freed him writes it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: The slave does not write a note. Rather, the one who freed him writes it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל gives the opposing view. The original master who freed the slave must take on the debt, not the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that the creditor is forced to free the slave. They disagree only about who owes the creditor the slave's value. The תנא קמא says the slave owes it, and רשב"ג says the original master who freed him owes it.

keyTerms.meaning: Not ... rather (this sets up a contrast)

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
The slave does not write;
rather, the one who freed him writes.
phrases.notes: Here that is the original master, since in this explanation he is the one who freed the slave.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אֵין הָעֶבֶד כּוֹתֵב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion on who writes the note.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The freeing master, not the slave, writes the note for the slave's value.

steps.title: What is the root of their argument?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which underlying legal principle the תנא קמא and רשב"ג disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move by asking what deeper principle is behind the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their argument is about who writes the note, but the גמרא wants to find the general rule behind it. Finding that rule ties this case to a wider topic in דיני ממונות.

keyTerms.meaning: A word that adds emphasis, often meaning 'actually' or 'is'

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי קָא מִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the argument in steps 1 and 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The general legal principle behind the disagreement over who writes the note.

steps.title: They argue about damaging another person's lien
steps.stepSummary: The argument depends on whether one who destroys someone else's lien (מזיק שעבודו של חבירו) must pay. רשב"ג says liable, and the רבנן say exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about one who damages his friend's lien. One master holds he is liable, and one master holds he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the argument depends on whether destroying someone's lien makes you pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By freeing the slave, the original master wiped out the creditor's lien on him. רשב"ג holds that damaging a lien makes you liable, so the freeing master writes the note. The תנא קמא holds that you are exempt, so the master owes nothing and the slave writes the note.

keyTerms.meaning: A lien, a creditor's legal claim on property set aside for a debt
Exempt, does not have to pay
Literally 'master', used to mean 'one of the Sages'

steps.whyThisMatters: This links the slave case to the general question of מזיק שעבודו של חבירו. That question comes up whenever someone destroys property that was set aside for another person's debt.

phrases.aramaic: בְּמַזִּיק שִׁיעְבּוּדוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ קָא מִיפַּלְגִי –
phrases.english: They disagree about one who damages his friend's lien –
as one master holds he is liable,
phrases.notes: This 'master' is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, which is why he makes the freeing master write the note.

phrases.english: and one master holds he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַזִּיק שִׁיעְבּוּדוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ קָא מִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The argument is whether one who damages another person's lien must pay: רשב"ג says liable, and the רבנן say exempt.

steps.title: Support: this argument was also stated elsewhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a statement that says outright that the question of damaging a lien is the argument between רשב"ג and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also stated: One who damages his friend's lien, here we have arrived at the dispute between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its answer with a statement from the אמוראים that says the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous step figured out the root of the argument by reasoning. Here an explicit statement confirms that the topic of מזיק שעבודו של חבירו is exactly this argument between רשב"ג and the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated (this brings support from a statement of the אמוראים)
We have arrived at (this case leads back to)
The Sages, here the תנא קמא

steps.whatToRemember: In the first explanation, the original master freed the slave. The argument over who writes the note depends on whether one who damages a lien must pay: רשב"ג says liable, and the רבנן say exempt.

phrases.english: It was also stated:
One who damages his friend's lien,

phrases.aramaic: בָּאנוּ לְמַחְלוֹקֶת רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְרַבָּנַן.
phrases.english: we have arrived at the dispute of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 4.
steps.raayaObject: That the argument in the משנה is about מזיק שעבודו של חבירו.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A statement of the אמוראים (איתמר) linking that question to the argument between רשב"ג and the רבנן.

steps.title: עולא: the creditor was the one who freed the slave
steps.stepSummary: עולא explains the משנה differently: the creditor freed the slave. By law this does nothing, but because people now think he is free, the original master is forced to free him, and the slave writes a note for his value.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: Who freed him? His second master. By strict law the slave is not obligated in מצוות at all. But for תיקון העולם, since he now has the reputation of a בן חורין, they force his first master to make him free, and he writes a note for his value.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא offers a whole new reading of the משנה, in which the creditor, not the owner, freed the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The creditor did not own the slave, so his freeing has no legal effect, and the slave is not obligated in מצוות like a free man. But once word has spread that he is free, the חכמים force the real owner (רבו ראשון) to free him for תיקון העולם. The slave then writes a note to pay his value to that owner.

keyTerms.meaning: The strict letter of the law
For the betterment of society (a rabbinic enactment)
A reputation has spread about him
His first master, meaning the original owner

steps.confusionAlert: In this explanation, the creditor did the freeing and the original owner is the one forced to free him. This is the reverse of the first explanation.

phrases.english: Ulla said:
Who freed him? His second master.
phrases.notes: The 'second master' is the creditor who held the slave as security.

phrases.aramaic: שׁוּרַת הַדִּין אֵין הָעֶבֶד חַיָּיב כְּלוּם בְּמִצְוֹת;
phrases.english: By strict law, the slave is not obligated at all in מצוות;
but for the betterment of the world –

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֲרֵי יָצָא עָלָיו שֵׁם בֶּן חוֹרִין,
phrases.english: since the reputation of a free man has spread about him,
they force his first master
and he makes him a free man,
and he writes a note for his value.
phrases.notes: The slave writes it, promising to pay the original master, who had to free him without being paid.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּלָּא אָמַר: מִי שִׁיחְרְרוֹ – רַבּוֹ שֵׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the case in the משנה from the one in steps 1 to 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the creditor freed the slave, it has no legal effect. But because of the rumor, the original master is forced to free him, and the slave writes a note for his value.

steps.title: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in עולא's reading: the creditor who freed him writes
steps.stepSummary: In עולא's reading, רשב"ג says the slave does not write the note. The creditor who freed him writes it and pays the original master.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: He (the slave) does not write. Rather, the one who freed him writes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes עולא's reading by explaining רשב"ג's view in this new case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording of רשב"ג stays the same, but now 'the one who freed him' means the creditor. He caused the original master to lose his slave, so according to רשב"ג he is the one who must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not write (meaning the slave)
Writes, meaning he takes on the debt in writing

steps.whatToRemember: There are two readings of the משנה. In the first, the original master freed the slave, and the creditor is forced to free him. In עולא's reading, the creditor freed him, and the original master is forced to free him. In both readings, רשב"ג puts the payment on whoever did the freeing.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
He does not write;
rather, the one who freed him writes.
phrases.notes: In עולא's reading, 'the one who freed him' is the creditor.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ כּוֹתֵב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes עולא's reading with רשב"ג's opposing view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In עולא's reading, the creditor who freed the slave writes the note, not the slave.

steps.title: What is the argument about in עולא's reading?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which legal principle רשב"ג and the תנא קמא disagree about, according to עולא's explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks, inside עולא's reading, what the real argument is between רשב"ג and the תנא קמא. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב's reading, the argument was about destroying a lien (step 4). In עולא's reading the creditor freed the slave, so that answer may no longer fit. The גמרא wants to know what principle stands behind the argument now.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the principle behind the dispute in עולא's version, which was described in steps 6-7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying legal principle of the dispute in עולא's reading.

steps.title: They argue about damage that cannot be seen
steps.stepSummary: The argument is about היזק שאינו ניכר. רשב"ג holds that it counts as damage, so the creditor pays. The תנא קמא holds that it does not count as damage, so the creditor is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about damage that is not visible. One master holds that it is called damage, and the other master holds that it is not called damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the argument is about damage nobody can see. The slave looks exactly the same, but the master lost him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The creditor's act did nothing physical to the slave. It only made people think the slave was free, and that forced the master to free him. רשב"ג says this kind of hidden loss still counts as damage, so the creditor pays. The תנא קמא says it does not count, so he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage that cannot be seen: the item looks the same but has lost value
It is called damage, so the one who caused it is liable

steps.whatToRemember: In רב's reading the dispute is about destroying a lien. In עולא's reading it is about damage that cannot be seen.

phrases.english: They disagree about damage that is not visible:
One master holds it is called damage,
phrases.notes: This is רשב"ג, so the creditor pays.

phrases.english: and the other master holds it is not called damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּהֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree about whether damage that cannot be seen counts as damage. רשב"ג says yes, and the תנא קמא says no.

steps.title: Why didn't עולא explain the משנה like רב?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why עולא rejected רב's reading, in which the master himself freed the mortgaged slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא: what is the reason he did not say like רב?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now compares the two readings. It asks what bothered עולא about רב's explanation, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב read the משנה as a case where the real owner freed the slave. עולא read it as a case where the creditor freed him. The גמרא wants to know what made עולא leave the simpler-looking reading.

phrases.english: עולא, what is the reason
that he did not say like רב?

steps.triggerLanguage: עוּלָּא, מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָמַר כְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining עולא's reading to asking why he rejected רב's reading.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What in the משנה pushed עולא away from רב's reading.

steps.title: עולא: the creditor cannot be called "his master"
steps.stepSummary: עולא could answer: in רב's reading, the person the משנה forces to free the slave ("כופין את רבו") is the creditor. But the creditor never owned the slave, so the משנה could not call him "his master."
steps.simpleTranslation: He would say to you: the second one, do you call him "his master"?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives עולא's reason, which is a word in the משנה. The משנה says "his master" freed the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב's reading the owner freed the slave, so the one forced to free him ("רבו") must be the creditor, the רבו שני. עולא objects that the creditor only holds a lien and was never the slave's master. So he reads the case the other way: the creditor did the freeing, and the real owner, who truly is "his master," is the one forced.

keyTerms.meaning: The second one: the other person in the case
His master, the word the משנה uses

steps.confusionAlert: Each side reads the word "רבו" (or "משחרר") a little differently. Just remember the main point: עולא's proof comes from the word "master," and רב's proof comes from the word "frees."

phrases.english: He would say to you: the second one,
phrases.notes: The second one is the creditor. In רב's reading the משנה would be calling him "his master," but he never owned the slave.

phrases.english: do you call him "his master"?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ: שֵׁנִי – רַבּוֹ קָרֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10 by pointing to the word "רבו" in the משנה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word "רבו" does not fit רב's reading, so עולא explains it differently.

steps.title: Why didn't רב explain the משנה like עולא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks the opposite question: why did רב reject עולא's reading, in which the creditor freed the slave?
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב: what is the reason he did not say like עולא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the question around and asks what bothered רב about עולא's reading. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each אמורא needs a reason for not taking the other reading. The גמרא now looks for רב's reason, which balances the challenge it gave for עולא.

phrases.english: And רב, what is the reason
that he did not say like עולא?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב, מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָמַר כְּעוּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks the same question as step 10, now about רב.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What in the משנה pushed רב away from עולא's reading.

steps.title: רב: the משנה says the slave was really "freed"
steps.stepSummary: רב could answer: in עולא's case the creditor's act frees nothing, so the משנה would not call it "freeing." So the real owner must have done the freeing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would say to you: the second one, do you call him "one who frees"?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רב's reason, which also comes from a word in the משנה: the slave was "freed."
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא himself admitted (step 6) that by law the creditor's act does nothing, because the creditor does not own the slave. רב says the משנה would not use the word "freed" for an act that does not work. So he reads the case as the owner freeing him, which really does work.

keyTerms.meaning: One who frees a slave, with a release that actually works

steps.whatToRemember: Each reading pulls on a different word. "His master" supports עולא, and "frees" supports רב.

phrases.english: He would say to you: the second one,
phrases.notes: Here the second one is the creditor. He does not own the slave, so his freeing does not work by law.

phrases.english: do you call him "one who frees"?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ: שֵׁנִי – מְשַׁחְרֵר קָרֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12 by pointing to the word "freeing" in the משנה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The creditor's act is not real freeing, so the משנה's word "freed" fits only רב's reading.

steps.title: A mortgaged field washed away by a river
steps.stepSummary: A new dispute: a man made his field an אפותיקי for a creditor, and a river washed it away. רבי יוחנן (quoted by אמי שפיר נאה) says the creditor cannot collect from the debtor's other property. אבוה דשמואל says he can.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: one who makes his field an אפותיקי for others, and a river washed it away. אמי שפיר נאה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: he does not collect from other property. And אבוה דשמואל said: he collects from other property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new, related topic with "איתמר." It brings an argument between אמוראים about what happens when a field set aside to pay a debt is destroyed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the mortgaged slave, this case asks how strongly the debt is tied to the item that was set aside. רבי יוחנן's view treats the field as the only source of payment, so if it is gone the creditor loses. אבוה דשמואל's view treats the debtor's other property as still owing, so the creditor can collect from it.

keyTerms.meaning: Property set aside as the specific source for paying a debt
He collects from the debtor's other property

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the bigger question in this part of the sugya: whether property set aside for a debt is the only source of payment, or just one part of the debtor's general obligation.

phrases.english: It was stated: one who makes his field a designated payment for others,
and a river washed it away;

phrases.aramaic: אַמֵּי שַׁפִּיר נָאֶה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: אמי שפיר נאה said in the name of רבי יוחנן:
phrases.notes: "שפיר נאה" literally means "handsome and good-looking." It is a nickname for this חכם.

phrases.english: he does not collect from other property;
and שמואל's father said:
he collects from other property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: הָעוֹשָׂה שָׂדֵהוּ אַפּוֹתֵיקֵי לַאֲחֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, related dispute about property set aside for a debt (an אפותיקי) that is destroyed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: if the field set aside for the debt is destroyed, the creditor cannot collect from the debtor's other property. אבוה דשמואל: he can.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק cannot accept אמי's ruling as stated
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק makes a pun on אמי's nickname: just because he is called 'beautiful,' should he say rulings that are not beautiful?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Because אמי is 'שפיר נאה' (beautiful), should he say teachings that are not beautiful?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק attacks the ruling quoted in the name of אמי שפיר נאה, that the creditor cannot collect from the debtor's other property. He finds it hard to believe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a play on words. אמי is called 'beautiful,' yet his ruling seems 'not beautiful,' meaning not correct. Normally a creditor can collect from any of the debtor's property, so why should he lose everything just because one field was washed away?

keyTerms.meaning: That are not beautiful, meaning not correct

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Because Ami is beautiful,
phrases.notes: He is playing on אמי's nickname 'שפיר נאה' from the previous step.

phrases.english: should he say teachings that are not beautiful?!

steps.triggerLanguage: משום דאמי שפיר נאה הוא, אומר שמעתא דלא שפירן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling quoted in step 14 in the name of אמי שפיר נאה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling (quoted by אמי שפיר נאה) that a creditor cannot collect from other property after the אפותיקי field is flooded.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A creditor normally can collect from all of the debtor's property, so losing the designated field should not wipe out the debt.

steps.title: אמי's ruling refers to a case where the debtor limited payment to that field
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק reinterprets the ruling: it is about a debtor who said, 'You will be paid only from this field.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Explain his teaching as a case where the debtor said to him: 'You will have payment only from this field.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק saves the ruling by limiting it to a special case. There, the debtor explicitly told the creditor that this field was his only source of payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a regular אפותיקי the field is just a guarantee, and the debt still rests on all of the debtor's property. If the creditor agreed to be paid only from this field, then once it is gone he has nothing else to collect from. So the ruling is correct, but only for that case.

phrases.english: Explain his teaching
as a case where he said to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the debtor, speaking to the creditor.

phrases.english: 'You will have payment only from this one.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תתרגם שמעתיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in step 15 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the ruling is about a debtor who said payment would come only from this field.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אמי's ruling seemed to apply to every אפותיקי, so the creditor would lose out unfairly.
steps.terutzMaskana: In an ordinary אפותיקי the creditor collects from other property. He loses only when he agreed to be paid from this field alone.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the distinction
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules exactly this way. Normally the creditor collects from other property, but not if the debtor said 'only from this field.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught so: One who makes his field an אפותיקי for another, and a river washed it away, the creditor collects from other property. But if the debtor told him, 'You will have payment only from this field,' he does not collect from other property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that matches רב נחמן בר יצחק's explanation word for word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spells out both halves. In a regular אפותיקי the debt survives the field's loss. If payment was limited to that field, the debt is lost with it. This confirms both that אבוה דשמואל is right about the normal case and that אמי's ruling fits the special case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way (a ברייתא supports this)

steps.whatToRemember: A regular אפותיקי is only a guarantee, and the creditor can still collect from other property. Only if the debtor said 'you will be paid only from this' is the creditor limited to that field.

phrases.english: It is also taught so:
One who makes his field a designated repayment for another,
and a river washed it away –
he collects from other property.
But if he said to him:
'You will have payment only from this one' –
he does not collect from other property.

steps.triggerLanguage: תניא נמי הכי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the explanation given in step 16.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's distinction between an ordinary אפותיקי and one limited to 'only from this.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that states both rulings explicitly.

steps.title: Another ברייתא: a creditor versus a woman's כתובה
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא says that both a creditor and a woman collect from other property. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says only the creditor does, because a woman does not go around to the courts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: One who makes his field an אפותיקי for a creditor or for his wife's כתובה, they collect from other property. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: A creditor collects from other property, but a woman does not collect from other property, because it is not a woman's way to go around to the courts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related ברייתא that adds a new case, an אפותיקי for a woman's כתובה. Here, as רש״י explains, the field was not washed away; the owner may sell it, and then the debt is collected from his other property. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל treats it differently from an ordinary debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion treats a creditor and a woman the same: both collect from other property: if the owner sells the designated field, they collect from the rest of his property. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the woman does not need to turn to other property, because she collects from the designated field itself. His reason is that women do not usually go back and forth to court, so the field was set aside as a fixed source for her.

keyTerms.meaning: To go around to the courts

steps.confusionAlert: This case is about a designated field the owner sells, not one washed away by a river. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is not saying the woman gets less. Her claim is tied to that particular field, since she is not expected to chase payment in court.

phrases.english: Another ברייתא teaches:
One who makes his field a designated repayment
for a creditor or for a woman's כתובה –
they collect from other property.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
A creditor collects from other property,
a woman does not collect from other property –
since it is not the way of a woman
to go around to the courts.

steps.triggerLanguage: תניא אידך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related ברייתא that adds the case of a כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first opinion: both a creditor and a woman collect from other property. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: a creditor does, but a woman's claim is tied to the designated field, because women do not usually go to court.

steps.title: New משנה: a half-slave splits his days
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: a person who is half-slave and half-free works one day for his master and one day for himself, according to בית הלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who is half-slave and half-free works for his master one day and for himself one day. These are the words of בית הלל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new משנה about a slave who belongs to two owners, and only one of them freed his half. בית הלל give their solution: he splits his time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects back to the earlier topic of freeing a slave. A half-slave is half owned and half free. בית הלל divide his work evenly: one day he works for his master, the next day for himself.

phrases.english: משנה: One who is half-slave
and half-free –
works for his master one day,
and for himself one day;
these are the words of בית הלל.

steps.triggerLanguage: מתני׳ מי שחציו עבד וחציו בן חורין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה, so the topic changes from אפותיקי to the half-slave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית הלל: a half-slave serves his master one day and himself one day.

steps.title: בית שמאי: the arrangement helps the master but leaves the slave stuck
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי object that splitting the days solves the master's problem but not the slave's. He cannot marry a maidservant, because he is already half free.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית שמאי say: You have fixed things for his master, but you have not fixed things for him. He cannot marry a maidservant, because he is already half free.
steps.whatsHappening: בית שמאי push back against בית הלל's arrangement. They point out that the slave is left in an impossible situation. The משנה continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With split days, the master loses nothing. But the slave cannot marry: his free half may not marry a maidservant. The rest of בית שמאי's argument continues in the next part of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: You have fixed or arranged things for

phrases.english: בית שמאי say:
You have fixed things for his master,
but for him you have not fixed things –
to marry a maidservant is impossible,
since he is already half free;

steps.triggerLanguage: בית שמאי אומרים: תקנתם את רבו, ואת עצמו לא תקנתם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: בית שמאי challenge בית הלל's arrangement from step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: בית הלל's solution of splitting the slave's days.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The arrangement protects the master but leaves the slave unable to marry. His free half forbids him from marrying a maidservant.
